So you're from Brazil. What's it like? Like, beaches all year?
That's the stereotype, and it's true somewhere. But Sao Paulo is a city that has no beach at all.
Wait, seriously? I genuinely thought all of Brazil was coast.
It's a country where a four-hour flight still leaves you inside it. My hometown is about an hour from the sea, which is close by our standards.
Okay, that's already more than I knew this morning. What's the weirdest difference?
Our school year ends in December, which means my summer holiday is your winter. Christmas is a beach thing for us.
That is genuinely breaking my brain. Okay, one more: what should I eat if I ever go?

Before you go, a quick word about the culture fair in November. Every international student gets a table, and the table is the easy part. What I want you to prepare is five minutes of talking. Not a lecture, and please, no history from a textbook. Bring one object, one photograph and one thing people can eat, and tell us why those three. The students who do this well are never the ones with the most information. They are the ones who explain something small properly. Last year a student from Korea spent five minutes on a school shoe rack and it was the best table in the room. Sign-up sheet is on my door until Friday.

Hi Lais, it's Beatriz again. You asked me about the culture fair thing, so here is my honest advice. Do not try to explain Brazil. Brazil is enormous and nobody can explain it in five minutes, and if you try you will end up saying the same three sentences everybody expects. Explain your street instead. I talked about the bakery on my corner, the one that sells pao de queijo at six in the morning, and about the fact that my school year ends in December, which broke everybody's brain here. Small and specific beats big and general every single time. And take food. Take a lot of food, and you will have friends by the end of the afternoon.

Lais signs up for the culture fair table on the sheet outside the teacher's door. She chooses one object, one photograph and one thing people can eat. She writes five minutes about the street where she grew up, not about the whole country. On the day she explains why the school year in Brazil ends in December. Three people ask her questions she has never been asked before.
